intro: A tree in a park weighs more than a car. A barn owl coughs up a ball of fur and tiny bones. A pond turns green in June and brown in October. All three are the same story told three ways. Something is catching sunlight and turning it into living stuff, and that stuff is being passed from one living thing to the next.

This unit follows that path. It starts with a doctor who weighed a tree and its soil and found that the soil barely changed. It ends with eagles coming back to the Mississippi River after people figured out what was breaking their eggs. In between you will trace food chains in a pond, a prairie and an oak forest, and watch matter go around in a loop that never ends.

By the end, you will be able to explain where the wood in a tree really comes from, why a field has thousands of voles but only a few owls, where a fallen leaf goes, and what happens to a whole web when one link is removed or repaired.
bigQuestion: Where does the energy in living things come from, and how do energy and matter move through a habitat?

timeline.t: Jan van Helmont's report on his willow tree is published: the soil lost only two ounces.
Joseph Priestley shows that a sprig of mint can restore air in which a candle has gone out.
Jan Ingenhousz shows that plants give off oxygen only in light, and only from their green parts.
Nicolas de Saussure shows that plants gain weight from carbon dioxide and water, not soil.
Charles Darwin describes an entangled bank where every living thing depends on the others.
Darwin publishes his study of earthworms, showing how they turn dead leaves into soil.
Charles Elton describes food chains and the pyramid of numbers in Animal Ecology.
Arthur Tansley gives a name to a place and its living things together: the ecosystem.
Raymond Lindeman shows how energy flows through a lake and shrinks at every step.
Rachel Carson's Silent Spring warns that DDT is building up in food chains.
The United States bans DDT; bald eagle eggshells slowly grow thick again.
The bald eagle, once down to about 400 pairs, is taken off the endangered list.

an invisible gas in the air that plants take in and animals breathe out
a gas plants give off and animals need to breathe
a stored form of plant food made of many sugars packed together
breaking food into pieces small enough for the body to use

test.q: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds. What happened to the soil?
choices: It lost only about two ounces
test.why: The soil barely changed, so the tree could not have been made from soil.

test.q: What was the gap in van Helmont's claim that the tree was made of water?
choices: He did not consider the air
He used the wrong kind of tree
test.why: He did not test whether the tree took anything from the air. Carbon dioxide was the missing piece.

test.q: Which gas do leaves take in to make sugar?
test.why: Leaves pull carbon dioxide from the air through tiny openings.

test.q: Priestley's mint let a candle burn again in spoiled air. What did the plant add?
test.why: Plants release oxygen, and a flame needs oxygen to burn.

test.q: Iodine turns dark on a leaf that sat in sunlight but not on one kept in the dark. Why?
choices: Only the lit leaf made and stored starch
test.why: Starch turns iodine dark. Only a leaf in light can make sugar and store it as starch.

test.q: Which food part stores the most energy in the same weight?
test.why: Fat stores about 9 calories per gram, more than twice as much as starch or protein.

test.q: How do tiny food pieces reach a muscle in your arm?
choices: The stomach sends them through the skin
They float up in the lungs
test.why: Digested food passes into the blood, which carries it everywhere in the body.

test.q: Which meal best fits the healthy plate guide?
choices: Chicken, rice, broccoli, grapes and milk
test.why: That meal has protein, a grain, a vegetable, a fruit and dairy.

test.q: Which of these is a consumer?
choices: A mold on a dead log
test.why: A grasshopper gets food by eating plants, so it is a consumer.

test.q: A field has tons of grass, thousands of voles and a few owls. Why so few owls?
choices: Only about a tenth of energy passes to each next step
test.why: So much energy is lost at each step that the top of a chain can feed only a few animals.

test.q: What makes a food web harder to break than a single chain?
choices: Most eaters have more than one food
It is drawn with thicker arrows
test.why: If one food runs short, animals in a web can switch to another.

test.q: What would happen to a forest floor with no decomposers?
choices: Dead leaves would pile up and their matter would stay locked away
test.why: Decomposers return the matter in dead leaves to the soil and air. Without them it piles up.

test.q: How is energy different from matter in an ecosystem?
choices: Energy cycles and matter is lost
Energy is lost as heat while matter cycles round and round
test.why: Energy flows through once and leaves as heat. Matter is reused again and again.

test.q: Wolves were removed from Yellowstone. Which change came next?
choices: Elk numbers grew and young trees were eaten down
test.why: Without their predator, elk multiplied and browsed the young willows and aspens heavily.

test.q: What did DDT do to bald eagles?
choices: It thinned their eggshells so eggs broke in the nest
It killed the fish they ate
test.why: DDT built up in the eagles through the food chain and caused thin, breakable eggshells.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is a tree made mostly of soil, water or air? Use van Helmont's numbers, Priestley's mint jar and what you learned about carbon dioxide and charcoal as evidence, and explain your reasoning.
tips: Start with a clear claim in one sentence.
Use at least two pieces of evidence: van Helmont's weights, the mint and the candle, or the black charcoal from a burned log.
Explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just what it is.
Say what van Helmont got right and what he missed, and why his test could not find the answer.
Mention where the tree's energy came from, not just its matter.
